name: Daybook
tagline: A daily journal and personal log app: write an entry a day, tag it, find it later.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: A journal is a text box, a date, and a search index, which is roughly the hello world of personal software. An agent can produce a local-first version with markdown entries, tags, full text search and a calendar view in a single sitting, and the data ends up in a SQLite file you actually own. The real product's advantages are the parts nobody enjoys building: a native mobile app you can write in from bed, sync across devices, reminders that fire, and an editor that feels nice enough that you keep the streak. If your journaling happens at a desk, the DIY version is honestly fine. If it happens on a phone at 11pm, you will quietly stop using it.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where each day gets one markdown entry, hashtags become filterable tags, and FTS5 search plus a year heatmap make old entries findable.
requirements: A machine you are willing to call the source of truth
Your own backup habit for the SQLite file
whatYouLose: Native mobile and tablet apps, which is where most journaling actually happens
Sync across devices without you building or renting it
Push reminders and streak nudges that keep the habit alive
Encryption at rest and the comfort of someone else worrying about it
An editor polished enough that writing in it feels good rather than tolerable
moatNotes: Journals compound. Three years of entries in someone else's schema is a soft lock-in even when the export button works.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because habit apps live or die on friction, and a hosted journal removes all of it: install, open, type, done, on every device you own. The feature list is replicable in an afternoon; the daily 30 seconds of zero resistance is not, at least not by you, at least not on iOS. People also pay for the quiet promise that the archive survives a laptop dying, which a local SQLite file does not make.
notes: The build is easy; the streak is the product.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal journal web app. Single user, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Next.js 15 (App Router) + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, database file at ./data/journal.db, created on first run
- No external APIs, no auth, no analytics

Data model:
- entries(id, date TEXT UNIQUE in YYYY-MM-DD, body TEXT markdown, mood INTEGER nullable 1-5, created_at, updated_at)
- tags(id, name) and entry_tags(entry_id, tag_id)
- An FTS5 virtual table over entry body, kept in sync with triggers

Features that are in scope:
- Today view at /: one markdown textarea for today's entry, autosave with a 1 second debounce, visible saved timestamp
- Hashtags in the body (#work, #running) are parsed on save and stored as tags; no separate tag UI
- Live markdown preview toggle, rendered with marked, sanitized
- /archive: reverse chronological list of entries with 200 character excerpts
- /entry/[date]: read and edit any past or future date
- Search box that queries FTS5 and highlights matches, plus filter by tag
- A 365 day contribution style heatmap on the archive page, colored by entry length, clicking a cell opens that date
- Keyboard shortcuts: cmd+k opens search, cmd+s forces a save
- Export: a button that writes every entry to ./export as YYYY-MM-DD.md files with YAML frontmatter for mood and tags
- Import: read any .md files in ./import with that same naming scheme

Explicitly out of scope: mobile apps, sync, sharing, encryption, images, reminders, multi user.

Ship a README with setup steps, a one line note that the only backup is copying ./data/journal.db somewhere, and a seed script that inserts 60 days of dummy entries so the heatmap and search are testable immediately. Put any config in .env.local, though it should need none.
